title: Self Host OpenCode 2.0: Setup Steps, Real Cost and Pitfalls
summary: Self host OpenCode 2.0 to run an AI agent yourself while renting the model per token. Know the setup steps, real costs, and pitfalls to avoid.
body_markdown:
## Run workflows around self-hosted OpenCode with Activepieces


### Workflow automation's role in the process


Don't expect Activepieces to host OpenCode; it's a separate automation tool, run in production by MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties, that handles the workflow around it.


It starts runs from a ticket or schedule, posts results to Slack (one of the 744 integrations in its MIT-licensed monorepo), and holds a human approval before anything merges.


After a rebuild, that matters, because the flow lives apart from the box and your triggers and approvals don't vanish with it.


The free plan on Activepieces Cloud allows unlimited flows and 1,000 credits a month, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so credits still limit how often the automation around the agent fires.


The flow calls an OpenCode server on a separate private network, and the output goes to a Slack channel and then a human approval step before merge.


Because a run is 1 credit however many steps it has, the call to the server and the Slack post cost 1 credit together, not one each.


Take from it that the agent never merges its own work, and the only thing crossing the network boundary is the request.


Read next to it, the flow shows where each piece of risk sits.


### What you host and what the workflow calls


When a run goes wrong, the cost is the edits it makes with the access you granted. OpenCode is an open-source coding agent that reads a repository, proposes edits and runs commands, using whichever model key you give it.


You host the server that runs the agent, the client that talks to it, and the config that says which models and permissions apply.


Activepieces only calls the server. Put the model keys in that config, with a budget on each, so a looping workflow can't drain an account.


Activepieces has its own AI keys option from the Plus plan at $20 a month, but that is for steps inside its flows; the keys OpenCode uses stay in your config, on your provider bill, which means compromising your repository compromises your cloud credentials.


### Where to start self-hosting OpenCode, or skip it


Teams run it on a shared dev box, in CI, or as a remote session they connect to.


Activepieces suits the recurring cases: a new bug ticket, a nightly dependency check.


Flows are unlimited on every plan, including free, but at 1 credit a run the free plan's 1,000 credits a month cover only 1,000 runs, so credits limit how often one fires.


If a workflow fires on every ticket, your model bill multiplies by every ticket, and the budgeted key is the only brake, so start with one ticket type.


On your own install, check the changelog before following any guide, including this one. Confirm which version you run, since config and server behavior may differ from older tutorials.


If you're one developer starting sessions by hand, skip Activepieces, even though the free plan costs $0 and includes 1,000 credits a month. Price isn't the obstacle: you gain nothing from automation until the same task recurs and someone else needs to approve it.
